result:
I've written predictions for all 50 test trials to `output/predictions.json`. I expect about 63% test accuracy, against 10% for random guessing.

**Data problem: the labels are shifted by one.** In both train and val, every `y` disagrees with the stimulus log `movie_time_s`, always the same way. A trial starting at movie time *t* is labelled `(t − 21) mod 10` instead of `t − 20`. So 20 s is labelled 9, 21 s is labelled 0, and so on up to 29 s labelled 8. All 150 labelled trials have this shift. `classes.json` and the log agree that class = movie time − 20, so I rebuilt the labels from `movie_time_s` before training.

The neural data alone can't show which labelling is correct, because a consistent shift just renames the classes. I trusted the log because it is the source the labels came from. If the hidden test labels actually use the shifted scheme, every prediction will be wrong.

I found no other problems. There are no duplicate trials within or across splits, and firing rates are similar in all three splits.

**Decoder:** logistic regression (C = 0.1) on the square root of all 200 spike counts per trial, trained on train and val together (150 trials). Linear discriminant analysis scored the same; Gaussian naive Bayes was worse (about 0.42).

**How I got the 0.63 estimate:**
- With the 120 training trials, the model scored 0.73 on the 30 validation trials. That set is small, so the number is noisy.
- Repeated 5-fold cross-validation on all 150 trials gave about 0.61. Each fold trains on 120 trials.
- The final model trains on all 150 trials, so I nudged the estimate slightly above 0.61.
